title: A 60-Year-Old Theory About Ants, Bees, and Wasps May Be Wrong
summary: Why do ants, bees, and some wasps live in highly organized colonies with a queen and workers? For over 60 years, the leading explanation was a genetic quirk called haplodiploidy. In these insects, females develop from fertilized eggs and have two sets of chromosomes, while males develop from unfertilized eggs and have only one. This means sisters share more genes with each other than they would with their own offspring. Evolutionary theory suggested that females might gain more by helping raise their sisters than by having their own young, thus driving the evolution of eusociality—a system where only a few individuals reproduce and others work. But new research from Arizona State University, published in Current Biology, challenges this long-held idea. The team, led by PhD student Sachin Suresh, analyzed social behavior and genetics across nearly 69,000 insect species using advanced statistical methods. At first, the data seemed to support the old theory: eusociality appeared more often in haplodiploid insects. However, when they looked closer, nearly all of that pattern came from a single group: the aculeate Hymenoptera, which includes stinging wasps, bees, and ants. Outside that group, haplodiploid insects were no more likely to evolve eusociality than other insects. 'When we formally tested it, we found there is no real association between the genetic determination system and eusociality,' Suresh said. Instead, environmental factors and life-history traits may play a bigger role. This finding overturns a textbook idea and opens new questions about the evolution of complex societies.
why_it_matters: This finding overturns a long-standing textbook idea about how complex societies evolve. If environment and life history matter more than genetics, it changes how scientists study cooperation in insects and beyond.

keywords.explanation: A genetic system in which males have one set of chromosomes and females have two, because males develop from unfertilized eggs.
Threadlike structures in cells that carry genes; in haplodiploid insects, males and females have different numbers of sets.
A social system where only a few individuals in a colony reproduce while others work to raise the young.
A group of insects that includes stinging wasps, bees, and ants.
The biological rule that decides an organism's sex, such as whether an egg is fertilized or not.
Characteristics of a species' life cycle, such as how it reproduces, grows, and cares for its young.

background_read: Arizona State University in Tempe, a major public research university, has long been a center for evolutionary biology and the study of social insects, including ants, bees, and wasps.
Current Biology, the journal that published the new study, is a peer-reviewed scientific journal that covers the life sciences and often features research in ecology and evolution.
The old haplodiploidy idea grew out of kin selection theory, developed in the 1960s, which showed that animals can pass on genes by helping close relatives survive and reproduce.

In haplodiploid systems, sisters are unusually closely related, so researchers predicted that female workers would benefit more from raising their sisters than from producing their own young, thereby driving the evolution of eusociality.

Sachin Suresh, a PhD student at Arizona State University, led a large statistical test of that long-held assumption; the new work challenges the idea by showing the pattern nearly disappears outside the aculeate Hymenoptera, pushing scientists to look at environmental and life-history causes instead.

perspectives.description: They see the study as an example of science correcting itself when larger datasets and better statistical methods become available. The result clears space for new hypotheses about how eusociality actually arises.

They may argue that the study's broad statistical approach could miss genetic effects that operate in particular lineages. They want further tests before textbook explanations are rewritten, especially because the old idea was influential for decades.

They focus on the risk of overgeneralizing from one insect group, since the pattern nearly disappears outside the aculeate Hymenoptera. This highlights the need for comparative methods that account for shared evolutionary history.

They plan to test environmental and life-history factors such as nesting, food availability, and colony founding. Understanding these causes could help explain why complex societies emerge in some species and not others.
